articles.title: Anal fisting 101: How to feel good and play safe
articles.description: Sex can be amazing in all its forms, but once you’ve mastered fingering , handjobs , and anal sex , you might be curious about trying anal fisting. Considering sex education has been gutted in the United States, and LGBTQ+ inclusion is villainized by Republicans, you probably weren’t taught much of anything about queer sex, and absolutely nothing about how to try a more taboo sex act safely. The transgressive nature of anal fisting can be a turn-on for both the giver and receiver, and the close communication and time necessary to do it without pain or injury means that anal fisting can feel more intimate than other forms of sex. But there are also risks involved, which is why you need expert advice from medical professionals and LGBTQ+ people who have experience with anal fisting before you start experimenting. What is anal fisting? Anal fisting is a form of penetrative anal play where a person puts their entire hand in their partner’s rectum. Despite the name of the sex act, most of the time, you won’t be inserting a closed fist, although you can work up to that if it’s your goal, according to Dr. Evan Goldstein , one of the leading anal health experts in the country who founded Future Method , a sexual wellness brand dedicated to revolutionizing anal sex prep. “More commonly, the fingers are typically brought together in a tapered shape that resembles a duck bill,” he tells Out . “Sometimes, to enhance the sensation, the fingers can be gradually opened only after the hand is comfortably inside. It is considered an advanced sexual practice that requires weeks, if not months of preparation, specialized communication with clear cues, an extremely patient top, and utmost respect for the body's limits.” Good Vibes Sexologist Carol Queen says that you’ll need “so much lube and infinite patience” if you want to try anal fisting. Queen, who is a sex educator, has decades of experience on the topic. Her partner is a fisting bottom who started learning about this type of penetration in San Francisco bathhouses, like the Catacombs, which was devoted to nothing but fisting. Queen and her partner also taught fisting workshops from 1990 to 2015. “Fisting is not done by putting the hand into a fist shape and trying to enter that way,” she says. “It is also extremely slow and almost meditative practice for most people. There often isn't a lot of hand movement at all once inside the rectum; it will be so full that this itself is a lot of sensation.” Anal fisting is often thought of as a kinky part of gay male sex, but the beauty of this sex act is that everyone can give it a try since everyone has an anus. While those with a prostate can experience intense orgasms from anal fisting, they aren’t the only ones who may enjoy it. If you prefer not to have your front hole stimulated or penetrated, but you want deeper, more overwhelming sensations, anal fisting may be a sex act worth exploring. And apparently, it’s more popular than you may think. Lylli Dupéré, who is the head of community and creator success at RedGIF , a website that hosts short-form adult content, says that she’s “seen growing curiosity around the practice,” which has led to more than 15,000 anal fisting videos being uploaded on the platform. “That doesn't necessarily mean everyone is trying it, but it does reflect a broader trend of people exploring more diverse forms of sexual expression and seeking educational or aspirational content online,” she says. “As interest grows, it's more important than ever that people understand this isn't something to copy without preparation. Don’t forget that the best sexual experiences are always the ones built on consent, open communication, and respecting each other's boundaries.” Can you orgasm from anal fisting? “Ouch” may be the only word that comes to mind when you think about anal fisting, but it can actually feel euphoric when done right. “Some people enjoy anal fisting because of the feeling of fullness and deep pressure from the act,” Dupéré says. “For others, it simply isn't pleasurable, and that's perfectly normal. Some people can orgasm from anal stimulation alone, while others enjoy it alongside stimulation of other erogenous zones.” Anal fisting can lead to a powerful orgasm and a deeper “emotional closeness” with your partner, Goldstein says. “Some orgasm from prostate stimulation, from other stimulation happening at the same time, or simply from the overall intensity,” he says. “Others enjoy it without orgasming, and some don't find it pleasurable at all. There's no one ‘correct’ response and so much of the pleasure actually comes from the experience itself because it is so unique. You’re giving your entire body to your partner in ways very few get to experience.” This advanced sex act can be rewarding both physically and emotionally, but only if you take the time to do it correctly. “If anal fisting is done with exquisite care, it can feel amazing,” Queen says. “People can indeed orgasm that way. If it is not done with exquisite care, it is not only hazardous but also painful. And in this context, pain is a danger sign, not just a sensation.” What are the risks? There are real risks involved with anal fisting that should be taken into consideration before you ever give it a try. The sex act can cause severe anal fissures, anal prolapse, damage to the rectum, and even injury so profound it can lead to death if not treated immediately. Queen calls anal fisting "the most complicated and dangerous sex act most people will ever perform" and says this isn’t “scaremongering” because the risks are real and need to be taken seriously when you’re deciding whether or not to give it a try. If you're not already part of a kink scene, Queen recommends finding a local fisting play community so that you can get advice on how to do it safely from people who have years of hands-on experience under their belt. Getting your partner prepared for anal fisting is already challenging, but you also need to be just as careful when exiting your partner’s anal canal as when you enter. “Removing the hand must also be done incredibly slowly so as not to prolapse the rectum or otherwise hurt the person being fisted,” Queen says. “This is an intense requirement if they are in pain or panic.” Goldstein calls anal fisting an “advanced form of anal play” and cautions that what you see in adult films isn’t realistic. “Social media and porn create unrealistic expectations about what bodies ‘should’ be able to do,” he says. "Anatomy varies — some people naturally have more accommodating pelvic floor muscles, others will always be tighter — and trying to match someone else's capability instead of respecting your own body's limits is one of the fastest ways to get hurt.” What should you do if you want to try anal fisting? Before you start down the road of preparing your body or your partner’s body to take a fist, you first need to be a seasoned pro at bottoming. “The person must be comfortable relaxing fully, and with communicating with the fister to stop,” Queens says. “If the two are in a dom/sub relationship this can be hard for some people, but it's a must. Anal sex isn't supposed to hurt, and if it does, info must be shared (and heard!) to change the speed, get more lube, check for harm, etc. When the fisting-bottom-to-be is comfortable with multiple fingers in their butt (three or four) and large-diameter toys, fisting play is then on the horizon. Finally, if they are not downright enthusiastic about learning to be a fisting bottom, this isn't the right play scene for them.” Goldstein says that it’s a mistake to rush things, because your anal tissue and all three anal sphincters need time to adapt and relax before you can take on anal fisting without injury. “Think weeks of consistent training, not one enthusiastic weekend,” he says. Someone who wants to try anal fisting for the first time should start with more traditional anal play and bottoming before moving on to dilators and larger silicone cones, “which teaches the skin to expand right alongside the muscle,” and then progressively larger dildos and training toys, Goldstein recommends. “Treat this all like dilation training: a consistent schedule, a little further each session, never forcing the next size,” he says. “At Bespoke Surgical, the patients who are into fisting tend to be some of the most in tune with their own bodies, because the cost of ignoring a warning sign is higher,” Goldstein says of his experience with patients at his practice. “And that awareness should continue long after the session. Your hole has been through a lot and deserves real aftercare in between sessions: rest, soothing suppositories and creams, and paying attention to how you're healing.” Expert tips for anal fisting Clean yourself out first Since you’ll already be experienced at bottoming before you try anal fisting, you likely already have a routine that works for you, but you’ll want to be extra careful before getting fisted because of the risk of tears and anal fissures. “Rinse out the anus first,” Queen advises. “Any lingering fecal matter will be a dire problem if an injury happens, so don't take the chance, at least until you are quite experienced.” But Goldstein also cautions that less is more when it comes to prepping your body. “Preparation matters too, but more isn't always better,” he says. "For routine anal sex, extensive douching usually isn't necessary and can irritate the lining if overdone. For deeper play like fisting, some additional prep is appropriate, but avoid excessive water pressure or repeated cleansing. A high-fiber diet combined with daily fiber supplements (like Future Method’s dual-fiber blend) do more for a clean, easy session than aggressive douching ever will.” Have a safe word Communication is going to be the key to doing this without the person being penetrated getting hurt. Pick out a safe word and keep communication open. “Set safe words before you start,” Goldstein says. “Red/yellow/green is the easiest system, since ‘stop’ can get lost in the moment for some people. And honor it every time your body signals it needs a break.” Queen says that the fister needs to know how to read their partner’s cues and the person being penetrated has to feel safe communicating openly and stopping play if things become painful. “Make sure your bottom feels comfortable communicating with you and assure them you are there with them and accept anything they say [or] experience, including ‘I need to stop,’” she says. “If your partner is eager to please you and prone to sub space, this is extra-important.” Take care of your nails Before your hand goes anywhere near your partner’s butt, you need to make sure your nails won’t hurt them. “You’ll need to trim your nails as close to the fingertip as possible and file them smooth,” Queen says. “Lick the fingertip to make sure there aren't sharp/scratchy parts left. Over that, it is wise to use gloves; use ones that fit you as perfectly as possible, because the wrinkles in too-big gloves, under that pressure, can irritate and hurt them.” A sharp or jagged nail is the fastest way to cause a tear, so take care of your nails to prevent this, wear gloves (this can even add to the experience if you or your partner has a medical fetish), and learn the proper way to hold your hand. “The fist shape inside the rectum is important because it allows you to turn your nails in toward your own palm rather than have them extended to any degree. The rectal wall should not be contacted with sharp nails under pressure, and pressure is what fisting gives,” Queen says. Lube, lube, and more lube When having any kind of sex, lube is usually a good idea, but with anal fisting, you’re going to need to pick a good lube and use way more than you think you’ll need. Have you coated your hand and your partner’s anus and rectum with lube? Good, now add more. “This requires more lube than you can even imagine in some cases,” Queen says. “It’s good practice to use a lube shooter or enema bulb to put some lube into the rectum before you start the finger penetration. Then you will likely need to add more as you go." She advises making sure you pick a lube that will hold up during a long session and works with the type of gloves you bought. “The slipperiest lubes are generally silicone- and oil-based. Vegetable shortening, aka Crisco, was a fave with fisters in the old days,” Queen says. “But choose your gloves (and, if you follow up with anal intercourse, your condoms) accordingly — you cannot use latex with oil-based lubricant, so you'll need non-latex safety gear if that's the lube type you choose.” Communicate more If you are the fister, you need to keep in mind that you have the ability to do irreparable damage if you’re not careful, so you need to pay extra close attention to how your partner is reacting to what you’re doing to them. “Watch and listen — breathing, body language, whether the muscle is softening or clenching, not just whether they're saying yes,” Goldstein advises. “Resistance instead of relaxation means stop, add more lube, and give it time before continuing.” And if you are the person being penetrated, don't agree to try this intense sex act if you don't trust your partner and feel comfortable being honest when something doesn’t feel good. “Say something the second anything changes, good or bad,” he says. “Your partner can't adjust to feedback you never give them.” Find a good position The more relaxed your body is, and the more space you can make in your pelvic area, the better, so figure out the best position before you get started. And don’t forget to breathe! “Get into a position that opens your hips and lets gravity help,” Goldstein says. “On your back with knees pulled up, side-lying, or a deep squat all work well.” You can even try relaxation methods you learned doing yoga. “Breathe like you're in a yoga class — long, slow exhales relax the internal sphincters far more than trying to consciously ‘let go,’” he says. Stimulate the prostate While you can reach the prostate with toys, fingers, or regular bottoming, you can provide intense stimulation with anal fisting. “If the person has a prostate, add extra pressure and a little movement in that direction and see if your partner likes the sensation,” Queen recommends. “You can also pull very gently backwards as though you are going to pull out — but with the fist closed you likely can't, but this small amount of movement might feel pleasurable to them. Ask!” Stay sober If you like to drink or are into chemsex, don’t mix either with anal fisting. It’s an extreme sex act, and the risks are so high that both parties should be stone-cold sober. “Never, never try it when either partner is drinking or party-drugging,” Queen says. “Because the plain truth is, there is no guarantee you won't hurt your partner — because you and your partner might not be fully informed about their rectal health, for example.” Don’t forget aftercare Once the session is over, make sure you “stick around for aftercare" if you're the fister, Queens says. You’ll want to not only emotionally support your partner as they come down from such an intense experience, but also make sure they “hydrate, maybe eat a little protein,” and then carefully keep “track of how the person is doing,” she says. What should you do if anal fisting is painful? If you’re experiencing a “gradual feeling of stretching, fullness, or pressure, along with mild muscle fatigue or a sense that the muscles are slowly softening,” that’s all completely normal and healthy, Goldstein says. He also explains that if you hit a “distinct pause point” which often happens around “the second sphincter or the recto-sigmoid junction” then it’s time to pause before continuing. But “sharp or stabbing pain, sudden intense discomfort, burning that keeps getting worse, significant bleeding, a sensation that something has torn, or numbness that doesn't resolve” are your body telling you to stop what you are doing and reassess before moving forward. “Stop right away,” Goldstein says. “Don’t try to push through it — pain is the body signaling that something isn't right. Pause, let the muscles relax, check in with your partner, and see whether the discomfort resolves. If it doesn't, end the session. If there's significant bleeding, persistent severe pain, or any concern for an injury, get evaluated by a health care professional rather than waiting to see if it improves." Queen has similar advice, but adds that if you have to stop because your partner is in pain, be careful how you exit their rectum. “Don't just pull your hand out,” she says. “You must exit the rectum the way you went in: slowly. You might need to add a little extra lube around your wrist. You may need to coach them through breathing deeply and reassure them that you are coming out as quickly as you safely can. Remember the rectal prolapse warning. This is when that is the greatest risk, and removing the hand fast, especially if a lot of the lube has absorbed, makes this a dangerous point.” Is there anything you can do if nothing is working? If you’ve been trying to build up to being able to take a fist, but your body just isn’t cooperating, that might mean anal fisting isn’t for you. But Goldstein says that there are a few things you can try before you give up. “And for people who've followed my advice to a T with consistent training and still aren't seeing much progress, that's not a failure on their part,” he says. “Anatomy can just be more resistant, no matter how disciplined the approach. In those cases, I'll often recommend anal Botox, which temporarily relaxes the internal sphincter so the tissue stretches more readily, paired with pelvic floor therapy so a trained therapist can work on the chronic tension or guarding that toys and dilation alone can't always reach. It's not a shortcut around the process, but rather a way to remove a physical barrier so the training you've already been doing actually has room to work.” Sources cited: Dr. Evan Goldstein is a leading anal health expert and owner of Bespoke Surgical and founder of Future Method .
